html:
What this is

The Symbolic World is a map of C. G. Jung's symbolic thought: 371 symbols, figures and concepts, joined by 1348 relations, resting on 1568 citations to his Collected Works. Nothing is here because a model said so. Every claim was proposed by one AI model and judged against its source paragraph by a second, from a different model family; an auditor from a different vendor re-reads each new batch in full, and 88% of all 1568 citations currently carry its stamp. Every claim keeps the receipt: the exact paragraph, a verbatim quote, and the record of who checked what.

Reading it: the stone (lapis) is claimed to be a projection of the self, Jung says so at paragraph 264 of Aion, and clicking the claim anywhere on this site shows the verbatim sentence.

One corpus

Everything comes from a single source: the Bollingen edition of the Collected Works, in English. No secondary literature, no commentary, no symbol dictionaries. That choice costs breadth and buys depth.

The bar along the bottom of the atlas is the corpus made visible: one segment per volume, sized by how much verified evidence it carries — the alchemical trilogy (CW 12, 13, 14) and Aion mined end to end, CW 9i in progress, five further volumes represented where the deep volumes reach into them. The segments select: click one and the atlas shows only that volume's claims.

Reading the atlas

Node colour is the kind of thing a node is. The palette borrows alchemy's metals — gold for concepts, silver for symbols, copper for figures, iron for operations, verdigris for substances, lead for motifs. Alchemy assigned its metals to the planets; mapping node kinds onto them is this project's design choice.

  • Search finds a symbol, a relation, a family, quote text, or a citation such as CW 14 §1. Typing offers completions, and choosing a symbol or a family opens it.
  • Click a node to read its connections; click a connection to open the claim itself — relation, quote, paragraph, verdicts. Copy link on any selection gives a URL that reopens it.
  • The chips beside the search box are the active filters — volume, family, voice, layer. Remove one with its ×.
  • The bar along the bottom selects volumes; each segment is sized by the verified evidence that volume carries.
  • Every citation shows a status dot: green, a person validated it; amber, machine-verified only — the honest default; red, publicly disputed with the dispute on the record.

How a claim gets in

Five stations.

  1. Propose. An Opus-family model reads a window of paragraphs and proposes claims, each with a verbatim quote.
  2. Check. A machine confirms the quote is letter-exact in its paragraph and at most 25 words, and that the relation is well formed. Failures are dropped, not argued with.
  3. Gate. A Fable-family model judges every claim against its full source paragraph. It is hostile by default: the claim survives only if the paragraph actually supports it.
  4. Audit. A Gemini model re-reads what survived, before any of it touches the graph. Universal for every batch since the Aion arc (mid-2026); earlier material was audited by sampling, and each claim's receipt shows whether it carries the stamp — 1374 of 1568 citations do today. When gate and auditor disagree, the auditor wins.
  5. Merge. The claim enters with its provenance stamped: dates, verdicts, corrections.

The rule underneath all five: the model that proposes a claim is never the model that signs it off. Proposer and gate are different model families (Anthropic's Opus and Fable lines); the auditor is a different vendor altogether (Google's Gemini); and the roles never swap.

The stations bite. In the most recent window, 73 proposed citations became 56 merged ones; the difference is what the checks removed.

Where people rule

Machines verify; people decide. Three places the human hand is in the record:

  • The gold set. 50 claims in the ledger carry a human-validated mark: a person read the source paragraph and confirmed the claim. This is the reference set the machine verdicts are measured against. Most claims are machine-verified only — the amber dot is the honest default, not a defect.
  • The dispute log. 19 public challenges to specific claims, each with its outcome on the record. A graph that cannot show you its corrections is asking for trust it has not earned.
  • The family layer. Relations are sorted into 25 families of meaning by two blind model arms. Where the arms disagree — 194 claims today — no model breaks the tie. The claim is marked pending review and queued for a human ruling, and every ruling lands in the ledger signed and dated, the same treatment the machine verdicts get.

Confidence levels

The checks are themselves checked:

  • Every one of the 1568 quotes is machine-verified against the corpus; the harness also carries seven deliberately corrupted claims, and all seven are caught on every run.
  • The family gate was calibrated by hiding planted errors among real assignments: it caught 19 of 19 in the first round, 20 of 20 in the second — naming the correct family every time — while wrongly flagging only 2 of 40 clean assignments.
  • The two blind classification arms agreed on 86% of 1347 relations. Twenty standing questions about Jung's thought are asked of the graph after every change; it currently answers 14 in full.

What the instruments do not cover, stated plainly:

Known limitOptions
One human reviewer; no second annotator yetIndependent second annotation with agreement statistics
A class of identity drift (two names for one thing entering as two things) is invisible to the current auditNo instrument yet — known gap, on the record
English translation only (Hull)German cross-check against the Gesammelte Werke

The paper

The method was published with release v1.3.0 — 248 symbols, 669 relations, 699 citations. That exact snapshot, atlas and ledger included, is preserved unchanged at /v1.3/, and the paper describes it. The live counts at the top of every page show how far the atlas has grown since, under the same gates.

The Symbolic World: Verification-First Knowledge Extraction from Interpretive Corpora (dataset, pipeline, and paper)
Spendel, Damian
